days.title: IAM Fundamentals
days.summary: Users, groups, roles and policies; identity vs resource policies with the real evaluation order — implicit deny by default, an explicit Allow grants, an explicit deny overrides every Allow, cross-account needs Allows on both sides; the six policy types, permissions boundaries, STS temporary credentials, MFA device kinds, Access Analyzer and key hygiene; monitoring with CloudTrail and credential reports. Summary, main concepts, flashcards, true/false and pop quizzes.

days.title: EC2 Compute Fundamentals
days.summary: What belongs on EC2, the four instance controls, launching and connecting (SSH, RDP, Session Manager), the instance lifecycle and status checks, and where EC2 sits on the compute spectrum; instance-type naming, AMI anatomy, user-data bootstrapping with IMDSv2, placement groups (7-per-AZ spread limit), tenancy and the 2024 public-IPv4 $0.005/hour change; plus VPC and load-balancing groundwork basics.

days.title: AWS Lambda Fundamentals
days.summary: Serverless: functions, the three invocation modes, memory-driven CPU (~1,769 MB per vCPU) and the 15-minute ceiling, request + GB-second billing with the permanent free tier, the hard quotas (memory 128 MB–10,240 MB, 6 MB sync / 1 MB async payloads, 4 KB env vars, 10 GB container images), async retries with on-failure destinations and dead-letter queues, reserved vs provisioned concurrency, runtimes/zip/container packaging, versions and aliases, execution roles vs resource policies, and Lambda vs EC2 on the compute spectrum.

days.title: S3 and Storage
days.summary: The EC2 storage trio (EBS vs EFS vs instance store), S3 object storage with 11-nines durability vs designed availability and strong read-after-write consistency, its seven storage classes with the fine print (30/90/180-day minimums, 128 KB minimum objects, per-GB retrieval fees) plus Intelligent-Tiering, versioning, lifecycle and CRR/SRR replication, Block Public Access, presigned URLs and the SSE options, the EBS deep dive (SSD vs HDD, gp2-vs-gp3 tuning, Multi-Attach, incremental snapshots), plus Storage Gateway, AWS Backup, FSx, EFS operating modes and Elastic Disaster Recovery, with clickable tier and type drills.

days.title: AWS Networking Fundamentals
days.summary: Amazon VPC from first principles: region-scoped isolation and your own CIDR, the three networking zones, subnets and tiers across AZs, route tables and the internet gateway, NAT gateways, stateful security groups (cross-group rule sources) vs stateless NACLs with the ephemeral-ports trap, the five reserved IPs and DHCP option sets, gateway vs interface (PrivateLink) VPC endpoints with per-AZ hourly billing, VPC Flow Logs, the two DNS switches, a hands-on two-tier custom VPC build, the inside-out troubleshooting checklist with VPC Reachability Analyzer, and where VPC peering, Transit Gateway and site-to-site VPN fit — with interactive pick-your-fix drills.

days.title: AWS Database Fundamentals
days.summary: Tables, attributes and tuples, primary and foreign keys; Amazon RDS with its five engines and 12-month free tier plus a hands-on EC2-to-RDS build, read replicas (read-scaling, promotable for DR) vs multi-AZ failover, and point-in-time backups vs manual snapshots; the NoSQL trio (key-value, document, graph) and DynamoDB with partition + sort keys, table classes and capacity modes plus the fine print (400 KB items, 4 KB/1 KB capacity units, Streams, Global Tables, DAX); the RDS-vs-DynamoDB comparison on schema, scaling, locking and cost; Amazon Aurora's cluster storage — six-way replication across three AZs, auto-growth to 128 TiB, writer/reader endpoints — and Serverless v2; migration with AWS DMS and SCT; and the in-memory pair, ElastiCache vs MemoryDB for Redis — with a pick-the-DB service-selection drill.

days.title: Understanding AWS Cost Drivers
days.summary: The five cost drivers — compute, storage, databases, data transfer, networking — and what each one's bill depends on; the pricing trio (free tier shapes, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans vs on-demand, plus Spot); Cost Explorer and Billing dashboards with cost-allocation tags, static thresholds and anomaly-detection alerts; the five provisioning decisions and right-sizing with Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer; manual vs auto scaling with spend caps; and the six classic overspending scenarios with their mitigations — with a pick-the-pricing-option drill. Plus a dedicated Cost Explorer quiz — the 12-month/18-month-forecast window story, grouping dimensions, the no-forecast-when-grouped rule, the hourly opt-in, 24-hour refresh and invoice-difference caveats, anomaly detection, RI/Savings-Plans utilization reports, recommendations and tag activation. And a separate AWS Budgets quiz — the six budget types, free monitoring (62 budget-days, then $0.02/day) with the first two action-enabled budgets free, IAM/SCP/EC2/RDS stop actions, the 8–12-hour refresh cadence against anomaly detection, and actual-vs-forecast thresholds plus the pre-created free-tier usage alert.

days.title: Understanding Amazon CloudFront
days.summary: Why a CDN exists — content close to the end user, with Amazon’s own research putting the cost at about 1% of sales per 100 ms of latency; CloudFront’s 2026 edge network as verified from AWS docs today — 750+ PoPs in 100+ cities across 50+ countries, 1,140+ embedded PoPs inside ISP networks and 15 regional edge caches; the full request flow: authoritative-DNS PoP selection, Host-header distribution mapping, cache behaviors matched by path pattern, then edge cache → regional edge cache → Origin Shield → origin; origins of every shape (S3, EC2, ALBs, API Gateway, MediaPackage, any HTTP server) with multiple origins, primary/secondary origin groups and private-subnet VPC origins; Origin Access Control over legacy OAI — the three signing behaviors, SigV4-signed requests and the cloudfront.amazonaws.com bucket policy with the distribution-ARN condition; distributions and the default catch-all behavior with the cache-key / origin-request / response-header policy trio; edge compute — CloudFront Functions (sub-millisecond, viewer events, millions req/s) vs Lambda@Edge (30 s, 10 GB memory on origin events, network and body access) vs the new Connection Functions inside the mTLS handshake; TTLs, invalidations and their in-progress limits; price classes; and 2026 pricing — pay-as-you-go with the 1 TB + 10M-requests + 2M-functions free tier, the new flat-rate plans (Free $0 · Pro $15 · Business $200 · Premium $1,000, no overage charges) and the up-to-30% Security Savings Bundle.

days.title: Week 2 Review
days.summary: Week 2 integrated on one interactive review page — the five sessions from Oct 26 to Oct 30: S3 and the storage family (EBS vs EFS vs instance store, seven storage classes with the 30/90/180-day minimums, 128 KB minimum objects and retrieval fees, versioning/lifecycle/CRR-SRR, Block Public Access, presigned URLs, SSE options, EBS gp3 tuning and incremental snapshots); Amazon VPC (subnets and tiers across AZs, route tables, IGW, NAT gateways, stateful security groups vs stateless NACLs with the ephemeral-ports trap, gateway vs interface endpoints and PrivateLink, the two DNS switches, five reserved IPs, Flow Logs, Reachability Analyzer, peering vs Transit Gateway vs VPN); databases (RDS's five engines, read replicas vs multi-AZ, point-in-time restore, DynamoDB keys/capacity/Streams/Global Tables/DAX with the 400 KB cap, Aurora's six-way cluster storage to 128 TiB and Serverless v2, DMS/SCT, ElastiCache vs MemoryDB); the five cost drivers with the pricing trio (Reserved Instances up to 72%, Savings Plans, Spot), Cost Explorer windows and Budgets actions; and CloudFront (750+ PoPs, 1,140+ embedded PoPs, 15 regional edge caches, the request flow, OAC's three signing behaviors, cache behaviors and the policy trio, CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge vs 2026 Connection Functions, 2026 pricing). 27 concept cards, 40 flashcards, 40 true/false, and three quizzes — the last a week-wide name-the-service drill. Review page format mirrors a day page.

days.title: Basic Navigation and Deployment Patterns
days.summary: Week 3 opens with navigation and deployment context from the Basic Navigation and Deployment Patterns course — the three infrastructure categories (Regions, Availability Zones, edge locations) with today’s live footprint verified from AWS (39 Regions / 124 AZs, minimum three AZs per Region, 2 more Regions announced, GovCloud US as two US-sovereign Regions); AZ names as account-relative labels vs AZ IDs that name the same physical location in every account (use1-az-style, the pin for cross-account zonal designs); Console and CloudShell as two views of the same region-bound context (default us-east-1, enabled regions only, sts get-caller-identity proving the shared identity, regional VPCs invisible across views); the four-box pre-deployment checklist (account, region, service, availability) applied to a public EC2 test web server launched end to end (test account for blast radius, us-west-2 for Pacific Northwest users, default VPC learning-only caveat, public IP, inbound-HTTP security-group rule, user-data bootstrap, no key pair); what a wrong-context deployment costs — vanished and duplicated resources, latency, data-residency violations, per-region pricing (t3.medium ~$0.042/h us-east-1 vs ~$0.067/h sa-east-1, on-demand Linux Shared, verified 2026-11-02) and metered cross-region and cross-AZ transfer; restoring the right context by AMI, volume snapshot or IaC redeploy; the five service families mapped to their scopes (compute regional, EBS zonal with mobile snapshots, S3 one-region placement under the global-namespace name rule plus the new opt-in account regional namespaces, VPC CIDR-overlap rule, IAM global-in-account, CloudWatch log groups regional with centralization); cross-account access as deliberate both-sides trust; and the vanished-resource trio: account → region → IAM permission — with the pop quiz, real-world picks and the where-does-it-live scope drill.

days.title: CI/CD and AWS Developer Tools
days.summary: Week 3, session 2 (CLF-C02: Deployment, Migration, and AI, Faye Ellis) — what CI/CD is and why it makes change easy: small frequent code changes integrated at least once a day (the exam cadence, matched by AWS’s whitepaper ‘at minimum once a day’) and the build-test-deploy functions automated so bugs are caught while small; AWS’s delivery-vs-deployment split (automated build/test/preparation plus a manual approval before production vs approval automated by pre-configured rules) with some teams delivering several times a day; the example workflow — local build and test, commit to the shared repository, then merge, build, re-test, package, and deploy automatically; the four developer tools mapped to their jobs — CodeCommit (a private Git repository in the cloud storing source, binaries, images and libraries, managing collaboration and version history; closed to new customers 2024-07-25 and reopened 2025-11-25 per the official docs history), CodeBuild (a fully managed build service compiling, testing, producing packages and Docker images from CodeCommit code), CodeDeploy (automated deployments to EC2, on-premises systems and Lambda — the docs add Amazon ECS with canary/linear/all-at-once traffic shifting — quick releases without downtime) and CodePipeline (the continuous-delivery service modeling, visualizing and automating every release step, triggered on every code change); and the CloudShell + CLI demo end to end — the browser shell with the CLI preinstalled and preconfigured, aws --version, aws s3 mb with a globally unique name, aws s3 ls, echo >> file.txt, cat, aws s3 cp, aws s3 ls bucket, the help pager (examples at the very end, q exits) and the version-2 CLI Command Reference organized by service.

days.title: AWS Monitoring Fundamentals (CloudWatch)
days.summary: Week 3, day 2 (AWS Monitoring Fundamentals — Neil Hitchins): telemetry monitoring — automated collection of data from remote sources into a central location at predefined time increments — with CloudWatch as the central repository for metrics, home of alarms and rules that action other services; which services send metrics (compute: EC2, auto-scaling groups, ELB, Route 53 health checks, Lambda; storage and content delivery: EBS, Storage Gateway, CloudFront; database and analytics: DynamoDB tables, ElastiCache, RDS, Redshift, EMR; plus SNS, SQS, SWF); the metrics hierarchy of namespaces and dimensions with per-instance metric examples — and the docs extras (no default namespace, AWS/service naming convention, metrics live only in their Region and expire after 15 months); basic monitoring (default, free, every 5 minutes) vs detailed monitoring (certain resource types, charged, every 1 minute — enhanced monitoring on Beanstalk, request metrics on S3); the CloudWatch agent (downloadable package, wide OS support, wizard, in-guest memory and page file metrics the defaults miss, installed via CLI or Systems Manager with configure-once reuse); CloudWatch Logs — log events into streams into groups, Standard vs Infrequent Access log classes (Infrequent Access is renamed Essentials in today's docs, and a log group's class is locked at creation), Live Tail and anomaly detection as Standard-class features, metric filters translating logs into numeric metrics, vended vs custom logs, and the three ways to send logs (agent, CLI PutLogEvents command, PutLogEvents API); CloudWatch alarms with the three states (OK, In alarm, Insufficient data) and push notifications via SNS topics + email subscriptions, no custom code; closing with the full first-alarm demo: a t3.micro EC2 instance loaded with the stress tool until CPUUtilization (threshold greater than 10% on a five-minute period) flips the alarm from Insufficient data to In alarm and the SNS email arrives — one out of the last one data point greater than the threshold of 10.

days.title: Asynchronous Messaging in AWS (SNS / SQS)
days.summary: Session 3 — a groundwork page built without a course transcript: every fact verified against live AWS documentation today (Nov 3, 2026) via API-backed search and fetch, and every cited link curl-checked before publishing. Topic: asynchronous messaging in AWS — the doc definition of a message queue (a form of asynchronous service-to-service communication used in serverless and microservices architectures; messages are stored until processed and deleted), and the two primitives for decoupling. SQS: fully managed pull-based queuing — producers SendMessage, consumers ReceiveMessage, process, DeleteMessage; standard queues (the default) run nearly unlimited API calls per second with guaranteed at-least-once delivery (occasional duplicates — keep consumers idempotent or dedupe by message ID) and best-effort ordering; FIFO queues deliver exactly-once processing and strict ordering (name must end .fifo — the suffix counts toward the 80-character quota; high-throughput mode reaches 3,000 messages per second with batching or 300 per second per operation); verified numbers — max message size 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes; the 256 KB figure is outdated), retention default 4 days, minimum 60 seconds, maximum 14 days (1,209,600 seconds); visibility timeout default 30 seconds, maximum 12 hours, zero releases a message to another consumer; short polling responds immediately but can return empty responses, long polling waits up to 20 seconds (fewer empty responses, lower cost); dead-letter queues via a redrive policy with maxReceiveCount. SNS: fully managed pub/sub push with topics as logical access points, spanning Application-to-Application and Application-to-Person messaging; subscriber endpoint types (Amazon SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, Email, Mobile push, Mobile text/SMS, Amazon Data Firehose, service providers like Datadog, MongoDB and Splunk); HTTP(S), email and cross-account subscribers must confirm subscriptions (pending up to 30 days); filter policies are JSON objects on the subscription selecting which messages a subscriber receives, keyed on message attributes (timestamps, geospatial data, signatures, identifiers); raw message delivery strips SNS metadata for SQS subscribers; message size default 256 KiB with AWS whats-new (Sept 18, 2026) raising payloads up to 1 MiB — a 4x increase — via per-topic MaximumMessageSize; SNS FIFO topics pair with SQS FIFO queues for ordered, deduplicated delivery; the fan-out pattern — one topic delivering copies of each message to multiple SQS queues for independent, asynchronous processing — and the choosing rule: SQS for one-to-one buffering, SNS for one-to-many push, SNS-into-SQS fan-out when broadcast plus durable per-consumer buffers are both needed. Fresh 40 flashcards, 40 true/false (page-internal dedupe clean, zero overlap with today's earlier pages), pop quiz, real-world picks and an 8-row which-service drill (SQS / SNS / fan-out).

Day 13 (AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner CLF-C02: Monitoring, Security, and Pricing — David Blocher; billing & cost module only): pay-as-you-go economics and the shared cost responsibility — moving to the cloud trades fixed expense for variable, and unattended waste is billed anyway; TCO thinking with the Pricing Calculator (estimate + CSV export); compute purchasing options: On-Demand pay-per-second/no commitment, Reserved Instances up to 72% on 1–3-year commitments (all/partial/no upfront), Savings Plans committing to dollars-per-hour across eligible families, Spot up to 90% interruptible with a two-minute warning for batch/flexible jobs; spend-lean compute habits — right-sizing, Auto Scaling to demand, dev/test environments off nights and weekends, Compute Optimizer ML recommendations; storage cost levers — S3 storage classes (Standard vs Infrequent Access vs Glacier tiers) with per-GB retrieval fees on archive classes, lifecycle policies transitioning to IA, expiring stale versions and aborting incomplete multipart uploads; data transfer rulebook — inbound free, outbound about ten cents/GB with the first 100 GB/month per account free (today's docs), cross-AZ and cross-region movement billed, CloudFront egress cheaper than EC2/S3; monitoring and predicting costs — AWS Budgets (actual + forecasted alerts by email or SNS; the $10 demo budget's three default alerts: actual 85% = $8.50, actual 100%, forecasted 100%, firing only after email verification), Cost Explorer (13 months history, 12-month forecast), and the most-detailed Cost and Usage Report (delivered daily to S3 in zipped files split at up to 500 MB, queried with Athena); multi-account billing — consolidated billing in AWS Organizations (one payer bill, pooled volume discounts, RI/Savings Plans sharing, member accounts track their own costs) plus Billing Conductor's custom billing views for resellers; tagging and resource groups with cost allocation tags activated in the Billing console; Trusted Advisor cost checks (idle load balancers, unattached EBS volumes; seven core checks on Basic support per today's docs); support — the course's legacy tiers (Developer $29, Business $100, Enterprise On-Ramp $5,500, Enterprise $15,000) flagged against today's docs: Developer/Business/Enterprise On-Ramp discontinued January 1, 2027, current lineup Basic (free), Business Support+ from $29/month (AI-powered, 24/7), Enterprise Support with designated TAM + 15-minute responses at a $5,000 minimum (was $15,000), plus AWS Unified Operations; beyond tickets — re:Post, Knowledge Center, AWS Partner Network, Managed Services, AWS Activate credits; exam framing: billing, pricing, and support is the smallest CLF-C02 domain at 12% of scored content.
